name: Oliver Cromwell
also_known_as: Lord Protector of the Commonwealth of England, Scotland and Ireland; 'Old Ironsides'
role: Puritan soldier and statesman; parliamentary general in the English Civil Wars and Lord Protector (1653–1658)

died.cause: Illness: recurrent fever ('tertian ague', probably malaria), with a kidney or urinary infection

summary: A Cambridgeshire gentleman and MP who, after an intense Puritan conversion, became the most successful general of the parliamentary side in the English Civil Wars. He helped bring Charles I to trial and execution (1649), conquered Ireland and Scotland, and ruled as Lord Protector from 1653. He gave wide liberty to Protestant sects and quietly allowed Jews to return to England, but banned the Prayer Book and Catholic worship. His army's massacres at Drogheda and Wexford (1649) and the confiscation of Catholic land in Ireland make him one of the most hated figures in Irish history.

key_dates.label: Enters Sidney Sussex College, Cambridge, a Puritan foundation
Elected MP for Huntingdon; around this time undergoes a religious conversion he later describes in a 1638 letter
Elected MP for Cambridge in the Short and Long Parliaments
Leads the cavalry at the parliamentary victory of Marston Moor (2 July)
Lieutenant-General of horse in the New Model Army; decisive at Naseby (14 June)
Signs Charles I's death warrant (executed 30 January); invades Ireland, storming Drogheda (11 September) and Wexford (11 October)
Defeats the Scots at Dunbar (3 September)
Dissolves the Rump Parliament by force (20 April); installed as Lord Protector (16 December)
Rule of the Major-Generals; calls the Whitehall Conference on readmitting the Jews
Refuses Parliament's offer of the crown but accepts a revised constitution, the Humble Petition and Advice

accomplishments.text: Built the disciplined 'Ironsides' cavalry and helped create the New Model Army, which won the First Civil War for Parliament at Marston Moor and Naseby.
Ruled England, Scotland, and Ireland as Lord Protector (1653–1658), the only non-royal head of state in English history.

Under the Instrument of Government (1653) protected the worship of Protestants of many kinds outside a broad national church, including Independents, Baptists, and others, while excluding 'popery and prelacy'.

Allowed Jews to live and worship privately in England from 1656, after the Whitehall Conference, called in answer to Menasseh ben Israel's petition, reached no formal decision; Jews had been expelled in 1290.
Saw himself and his army as instruments of God's providence; his letters and speeches are among the fullest records of Puritan piety in politics.
Drove the trial and execution of Charles I in 1649, an act he defended as God's judgment and his opponents called regicide.
Conquered Ireland (1649–1650) and Scotland (1650–1651), uniting the three kingdoms under one government for the first time.
Dissolved Parliaments that opposed him and ruled for a time through major-generals, leading critics then and since to call him a military dictator.

sayings_intro: A selection. Several famous lines credited to Cromwell come from later reports rather than his own writings.

original.phrase: "I beseech you, in the bowels of Christ, think it possible you may be mistaken."
original.reference: Letter to the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland, 3 August 1650

original.phrase: "I am persuaded that this is a righteous judgment of God upon these barbarous wretches"
original.reference: Letter to William Lenthall, Speaker of Parliament, after Drogheda, September 1649

original.phrase: "A few honest men are better than numbers"
original.reference: Letter of 1643 on raising his cavalry

popularized.reference: Reported request to the painter Peter Lely to paint him truthfully
popularized.note: First recorded by Horace Walpole over a century later (Anecdotes of Painting, 1764); the exact words are not in Cromwell's own writings.

misattributed.phrase: "Put your trust in God, and keep your powder dry"
misattributed.note: First found in a poem by Valentine Blacker published in 1834.

misattributed.phrase: "You have sat too long for any good you have been doing… In the name of God, go!"
misattributed.reference: Said to have been spoken when he dissolved the Rump Parliament, 20 April 1653
misattributed.note: The wording comes from later accounts, not a record made at the time; it was quoted by Leo Amery against Neville Chamberlain in 1940.

persecuted_others_note: Cromwell argued for liberty of conscience among Protestants and protected sects such as Baptists and, to a degree, Quakers. He excluded Catholics and Anglican episcopal worship from that liberty, and his campaigns in Ireland included massacres and a land settlement that dispossessed Catholic landowners. He sought leniency for the Quaker James Nayler in 1656 but did not stop Parliament's punishment.

persecuted_others.title: Massacre at Drogheda
persecuted_others.targets: The royalist garrison of Drogheda, Catholic priests and friars, and some civilians
persecuted_others.summary: After his summons to surrender was refused, Cromwell's army stormed Drogheda and, on his order of no quarter, killed most of the garrison of about 3,000 men, including the commander Sir Arthur Aston, and the Catholic clergy found in the town; survivors were shipped to Barbados. Cromwell's own letter calls it 'a righteous judgment of God'. How many civilians were killed is disputed: some historians, such as Tom Reilly, argue few were, while Micheál Ó Siochrú and others hold that many townspeople died.
persecuted_others.outcome: About 3,500 killed by Cromwell's own estimate; the event became central to Irish memory of Cromwell.

persecuted_others.title: Sack of Wexford
persecuted_others.targets: The garrison and townspeople of Wexford, including Franciscan friars
persecuted_others.summary: While surrender terms were being negotiated, Cromwell's troops broke into Wexford and killed some 2,000 soldiers and civilians, including friars. Cromwell had not ordered the assault but wrote that he did not intend to punish it, calling it God's just judgment.
persecuted_others.outcome: The town was sacked and many drowned trying to flee.

persecuted_others.title: Cromwellian settlement of Ireland
persecuted_others.targets: Irish Catholic landowners and their families
persecuted_others.summary: The Act for the Settlement of Ireland (1652), passed by the Rump Parliament and carried out under the Protectorate, confiscated most Catholic-owned land; many owners were transplanted west of the Shannon to Connacht and Clare, and thousands of Irish were transported as indentured labourers to the Caribbean. Catholic worship was banned and priests were hunted, with a reward offered for them.
persecuted_others.outcome: Catholic landownership in Ireland fell from about 60% before 1641 to under 10% by the 1660s.

persecuted_others.title: Scottish prisoners after Dunbar
persecuted_others.targets: About 5,000 Scottish soldiers captured at Dunbar
persecuted_others.summary: Prisoners taken by Cromwell's army were marched south to Durham, where some 1,500 or more died of hunger and disease in captivity under Sir Arthur Haselrig; many survivors were sold into indentured labour in New England and elsewhere.
persecuted_others.outcome: Remains of some of the prisoners were found in Durham in 2013.

persecuted_others.title: Bans on Catholic and Prayer Book worship
persecuted_others.targets: Catholics and Anglicans loyal to bishops and the Book of Common Prayer
persecuted_others.summary: The Long Parliament abolished the Prayer Book in 1645. Cromwell's Instrument of Government (1653) excluded 'popery and prelacy' from religious liberty, and a 1655 proclamation after the royalist Penruddock rising barred ejected Anglican clergy from teaching or preaching. Enforcement was uneven, and private Prayer Book services often went on.
persecuted_others.outcome: Episcopal worship and Catholic Mass remained illegal until the Restoration of 1660.

persecution_note: Cromwell was never arrested or tried in life; he was a soldier in a civil war in which he was repeatedly at risk of death or, had Parliament lost, prosecution for treason. After the Restoration his body was exhumed and 'executed'.

persecution.title: Posthumous execution
persecution.summary: On the twelfth anniversary of Charles I's execution, the restored monarchy's Parliament had the bodies of Cromwell, his son-in-law Henry Ireton, and the judge John Bradshaw dug up from Westminster Abbey, hanged in chains at Tyburn, and beheaded. Cromwell's head was set on a pole above Westminster Hall for about two decades.

responsible.name: The Convention and Cavalier Parliaments
responsible.role: Passed the attainder of the regicides and ordered the exhumations

responsible.name: Charles II
responsible.role: King under whom the order was carried out

persecution.outcome: The head passed through private hands and was buried at Sidney Sussex College, Cambridge, in 1960.

excommunication_note: Cromwell was never excommunicated by any church; he belonged to no single denomination and was a member of no church that disciplined him. He was posthumously attainted for high treason by Parliament in 1660, a civil, not church, sentence.
